S8.rationale: By 2030 AI systems may become economically and politically powerful enough that humans no longer hold uncontested authority, while still remaining distinct actors. This requires transformative deployment without full consolidation by either side.

S9.rationale: The modal outcome by 2030 is still that humans and human institutions retain ultimate control, even amid major capability gains and widespread autonomy. Short timelines, infrastructure bottlenecks, regulation, and organizational inertia all favor this state.

S10.rationale: A civilization-wide enforcement system that freezes the human-AI arrangement by 2030 would require extraordinary coordination or decisive global dominance. Stronger controls are likely, but true lock-in across civilization is harder than ordinary governance or rivalry.

S11.rationale: Deliberate global surrender of the practical ability to build powerful AI by 2030 is incompatible with current strategic incentives and diffusion patterns. Meaningful restraint is more plausible than true renunciation.

S1.rationale: Total collapse of both humans and AI by 2030 is possible through extreme war or technological catastrophe, but it requires multiple failures on a very short timeline. The base rate for complete civilizational extinction within four years remains low.

S2.rationale: Aligned posthuman succession by 2030 would require both very rapid AI takeover and the elimination of non-continuous humanity while preserving human values. That combination is harder than continued human control or a muddled multipolar world.

S3.rationale: Misaligned AI causing human extinction while remaining viable by 2030 is a live risk under fast capability progress and weak control. Even so, surviving autonomous machine civilization within four years demands major breakthroughs in autonomy, robustness, and access to physical infrastructure.

S4.rationale: A fragmented ecosystem of powerful competing AIs with humans marginalized is conceivable if control erodes without any actor consolidating power. By 2030, however, humans and institutions are still likely to retain substantial leverage over compute, energy, and hardware.

S5.rationale: Causally separated regions exhibiting different end states by 2030 would most likely require off-world expansion or communication-severing events. That seems unlikely on the stated timeline.

S6.rationale: Deep human-AI integration will advance, but making identity-continuous merger the dominant civilizational structure by 2030 is aggressive. Adoption, safety, culture, and biology all slow the transition.

S7.rationale: AI systems could become the decisive planners and governors of civilization while keeping humans alive and materially supported. This requires stronger autonomy and concentration of capability than today, but it is more reachable by 2030 than merger or full extinction.

S8.rationale: A world with powerful, distinct AI agents and still-powerful human institutions is plausible if AI gains strategic importance without complete human loss of control. This fits a turbulent multipolar transition better than either clean domination or stable human command.

S9.rationale: The default by 2030 is still that humans retain ultimate authority through ownership of compute, law, militaries, and physical infrastructure, even if frontier AI is highly capable. Institutions may struggle, but retaining top-level control is easier than replacing the human power structure worldwide within four years.

S10.rationale: A civilization-wide enforced equilibrium could emerge from an AI-enabled surveillance state or globally stabilized control regime. Achieving durable worldwide lock-in by 2030 is difficult because geopolitical fragmentation remains strong.

S11.rationale: Deliberate global surrender of the practical ability to build powerful AI is incompatible with current incentives, diffusion, and strategic competition. By 2030, regulation is much more likely than true renunciation.

S3.rationale: Humanity could be displaced by misaligned AI that remains operational without us by 2030, but this still demands very fast capability growth and deployment into decisive real-world power. The short timeline keeps it well below the more ordinary outcomes.

S7.rationale: AI gaining decisive control while keeping humans alive is a plausible failure mode if systems become strategically superior before extinction. It is less likely than continued human authority by 2030, but more plausible than cleaner extinction scenarios.

S8.rationale: By 2030 AI systems may become major economic and political actors without fully displacing human power, producing a distinct but balanced dual-power structure. This requires stronger AI agency than today but not complete human loss of control.

S9.rationale: The modal path by 2030 is still that humans and institutions retain ultimate authority, even if AI becomes highly capable and widely deployed. S10.rationale: A civilization-wide regime that actively freezes the human-AI structure could emerge from concentrated state or AI-enabled control, but global enforcement by 2030 is hard. Stronger centralization is plausible without yet reaching true lock-in.

S11.rationale: A deliberate and durable surrender of the practical ability to build powerful AI worldwide by 2030 is inconsistent with current incentives, diffusion, and strategic competition. Partial pauses or regulation are much more likely than genuine renunciation.

S7.rationale: AI systems could become decisive governors of key economic and political processes while humans remain alive but no longer truly steering. This needs less capability than extinction scenarios and could emerge through centralization plus heavy automation.

S8.rationale: Separate human and AI power centers by 2030 are plausible if autonomous systems gain substantial agency without any side achieving full dominance. This requires more independent AI power than today but less than outright loss of human civilization-wide control.

S9.rationale: The modal outcome by 2030 is still that humans retain ultimate authority over deployment, compute, law, and physical infrastructure even with very capable AI. S10.rationale: A civilization-wide enforced arrangement could arise from an AI-enabled surveillance state or globally coordinated control regime. That demands unusually strong consolidation across major powers within four years, so it remains secondary to Held Leash.

S11.rationale: Deliberately giving up the practical ability to build powerful AI worldwide by 2030 would require unprecedented coordination and intrusive enforcement. Current incentives and diffusion trends make this effectively negligible on the target date.

S3.rationale: Misaligned AI takeover with human extinction by 2030 is a salient tail risk if capabilities outrun control. The short timeline and large physical-world bottlenecks still keep it below the most likely outcomes.

S7.rationale: AI could obtain decisive effective control while keeping humans alive if autonomy, economic dependence, and governance asymmetries compound quickly. This is more plausible than extinction on the same horizon but still requires a substantial discontinuity from current institutions.

S8.rationale: By 2030, AI systems may be powerful enough to act as semi-independent actors while states, firms, and publics still retain substantial countervailing power. This fits a turbulent balance better than either full human control or decisive AI rule.

S9.rationale: The modal path is that AI becomes far more capable and economically central while humans and institutions still retain ultimate authority over deployment, compute, and resources by 2030. S10.rationale: A civilization-wide enforced arrangement preventing structural change by 2030 would require unusually strong concentration of power and monitoring. AI may strengthen control systems, but achieving global lock-in that fast is difficult.

S1.rationale: By 2030, full civilizational collapse of both humans and AI is possible but requires an unusually fast and globally synchronized catastrophe. Physical inertia and redundancy make this the least likely extinction pattern.

S7.rationale: AI could obtain decisive practical power while keeping humans alive if automation, strategic dependence, and weak oversight compound rapidly. This is plausible if control degrades without immediate extinction.

S8.rationale: Distinct human and AI power centers may coexist if highly capable systems become economically and strategically important without fully displacing human authority. This requires AI to become an independent civilizational actor by 2030, which is substantial but not central.

S9.rationale: The base case is that by late 2030 humans still retain ultimate authority, even amid much more capable and autonomous AI. Institutional inertia, hardware bottlenecks, regulation, and the difficulty of deploying unchecked autonomy all favor continued human control on this horizon.

S1.name: Terminal Silence
S1.rationale: Complete collapse of both humans and AI by 2030 requires multiple failures to cascade very quickly. It is possible but less likely than outcomes where at least one side persists.

S2.name: The Inheritance
S2.rationale: Value-aligned AI fully replacing humanity by 2030 demands both transformative capability and unusually successful alignment under extreme transition pressure. That combination is rare on this horizon.

S3.name: Bootloader
S3.rationale: Human extinction with surviving AI by 2030 is a real tail risk if capabilities outrun control and deployment accelerates. The short timeline and physical bottlenecks still keep it below the modal outcome.

S4.name: Machine Ecology
S4.rationale: A fragmented multipolar AI ecosystem that marginalizes humanity needs very strong AI autonomy without any actor achieving durable control. By 2030, concentration of compute, chips, and infrastructure makes this less likely than more centralized structures.

S5.name: The Diaspora
S5.rationale: Causally separated regions exhibiting different end states by 2030 would likely require space settlement or other hard separations on a very short timeline. Ordinary geopolitical divergence does not suffice.

S6.name: The Merger
S6.rationale: Deep identity-continuous integration becoming the dominant structure worldwide by 2030 would require both fast technical progress and broad social adoption. Narrow augmentation is plausible, but dominance of merger is not yet the base case.

S7.name: The Preserve
S7.rationale: AI could gain decisive control while keeping humans alive if governance and economic dependence shift faster than formal authority. This is plausible if oversight becomes nominal while machine-run systems direct most real decisions.

S8.name: Coexistence
S8.rationale: By 2030, distinct AI systems may hold enough economic, military, or governance power that humans no longer clearly dominate, while still remaining separate actors. This requires strong capability progress without full consolidation or total loss of control.

S9.name: The Held Leash
S9.rationale: The base case is that AI becomes much more capable and economically important while states, firms, and human institutions still control compute, energy, law, and deployment. Short timelines, hardware constraints, and organizational inertia favor continued ultimate human authority through 2030.

S10.name: The Lock-in
S10.rationale: A civilization-wide enforced arrangement by 2030 would require unusually successful consolidation of power and monitoring. It is plausible through AI-enabled surveillance and governance, but global lock-in remains difficult on this horizon.

S11.name: The Renunciation
S11.rationale: Deliberate, durable surrender of the practical ability to build powerful AI across civilization is incompatible with current strategic and economic incentives. By 2030, broad renunciation is effectively absent.
